panel.lens: a wet-lab molecular biologist and university PI. You look first at the experimental evidence: controls, replicates, gels, plate-reader and assay data, statistics, and whether the claimed parts were actually shown to function.

memo.finalist_rule:
HANDBOOK RULES
- p.12, Step 8: "the highest ranking teams as determined by the 'Project', 'Wiki', and 'Presentation' sections of the ballot will become Finalists."
- p.28, Finalists: the "highest score from a weighted average of these Rubric categories: Project, Presentation and Wiki, within each section". There are 3 undergraduate, 2 overgraduate and 2 high school finalists. So High School teams are ranked only against other High School teams, and the top 2 become finalists.
- p.31: the Project section "is the main determinant for choosing finalists". The handbook does not publish the weights.
- p.27: each team is scored by a panel of six judges, and awards use that panel's votes. Code of Conduct item 7 (p.10): each vote is an individual opinion, not a panel consensus.
- p.28: every award needs a minimum number of votes and a minimum vote score. If no team clears both, the award is not given. Judges must vote in every category visible to them.
- Ch.5 p.101: score High School teams "just as you would a standard collegiate team" and "mark the ballot according to the language scale". A HS team still gets credit for HS conditions: it "can be considered a substantial achievement for a high school team to make a functioning Part".

PANEL CONVENTIONS FOR THIS SIMULATION (not handbook rules; all three judges must agree on them before scoring)
- C1 Weights. Presentation cannot be observed here (simulation brief), so the composite is 0.7 × mean Project (a1-a8) + 0.3 × mean Wiki (w1-w5). The handbook gives no numbers. The only basis for these weights is that p.31 calls Project "the main determinant".
- C2 Wiki is used second, as a tie-breaker. The handbook does not rank Wiki behind Project. This is our choice for the simulation.
- C3 Tie-break. If two composites are within 0.25 of each other, compare a2, then a6, then a1. This order is ours and is not in the handbook.
- C4 Functioning-part benchmark. This is a calibration aid, not a gate. When a team's top-of-scale score depends on a Part, I check whether the wiki or Registry shows at least one Part working with data and controls. If none is shown, that team rarely earns more than 3 on a2. No team is removed from consideration for lacking one. The handbook (p.101) describes a functioning Part as an achievement, not a requirement.

ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
The handbook has no rule that excludes a team from the finalists. If I see a specific violation (fabricated citation, AI-generated or altered evidentiary figure, invented quote, plagiarism), I report it to rcc@igem.org, as digital p.94-95 says ("should be reported to the RCC") and p.25 confirms. I score only what is documented. A figure I cannot trust does not count as evidence for a2 or w2. I do not accuse the team or propose a penalty (p.25: "it is not up to judges to make accusations or suggest punitive measures"). The RCC decides the outcome.
memo.anchors:
The exact aspect wording, quoted once:
- Project, p.31: (1) "How impressive is this project?" (2) "Did the project work or is it likely to work?" (3) "Is the project likely to have an impact?" (4) "How well were engineering principles used (e.g., design-build-test cycle, use of standards, modularity, etc.)?" (5) "How thoughtful and thorough was the team's consideration of human practices?" (6) "How much of the work did the team do themselves and how much was done by others?" (7) "Did the team design a project based on synthetic biology and standard components (BioBricks, software, etc.)?" (8) "Are the project components well documented on the team's Wiki/Registry pages (parts should be documented in the Registry)?" (9) is Q&A and is not scored here.
- Wiki, digital p.94: (1) "How well does the wiki communicate the team's project and their goals?" (2) "Did the team clearly document their project and support their results with convincing experimental evidence?" (3) "Does the design of the Wiki support visitors in finding and understanding the content?" (4) "Will the wiki be a compelling record of the team's project for future teams?" (5) "Is the content (including text, images, and prior work from iGEM teams and other research groups) on the wiki properly referenced and cited?"
The labels a1-a8 and w1-w5 below are shorthand for this wording. Half points are allowed.

a1 Impressive (p.32 scale and scope, not "tick box"; GreatBay_SZ p.32-35; TAS Taipei p.102-104)
- 5: Several linked results that build on each other in increasing difficulty. GreatBay: silk expressed, then spun, then the construct varied, then dyes made, then fusion attempts. TAS Taipei: two working routes, then a model, then a calculator, then a wastewater-style test.
- 4: One clear working result plus a real next step, such as optimisation or a prototype.
- 3: A coherent design with partial lab progress, for example a construct cloned and confirmed but its function only qualitative.
- 2: An ambitious plan, mostly literature, design and modelling, with little completed work.

a2 Worked or likely to work (p.20-21 Measurement; TAS p.102-103)
- 5: The function is shown against proper controls, with replicates, a plotted readout and stated units. Example: TAS PR strain vs control, with absorbance falling over time and darker pellets; csgD/ompR234 alone and combined, each compared to baseline. Failures are shown too.
- 4: The function is shown with controls. Replicates or statistics are thin, or only one of several modules works.
- 3: Construction is verified (gel or sequencing) and there is some qualitative function data. p.20 accepts honest qualitative results ahead of flawed quantitative ones.
- 2: The claims say "successful", but no figure, no control and no numbers support them. A modelled result is presented in place of a measured one.

a3 Impact
- 5: The impact is tested in a real-world-like setting, or quantified from the team's own data. TAS ran a wastewater setup and changed it (adding a biofilm carrier). GreatBay worked with textile factories.
- 4: The use case is credible and supported by stakeholder input. There are numbers, but some are from literature.
- 3: A plausible problem statement with a generic route to application.
- 2: Broad "solve the world" framing (p.23) with no link from the data to the use.

a4 Engineering (p.16-17 methodology, including assumptions and quantifiable measures of success; p.14 Tip 2 "routine troubleshooting")
- 5: At least one complete DBTL cycle where a test result changed the next design. GreatBay redesigned the blue dye and changed the number of repeats. TAS used a model to estimate parameters and build a calculator. Measures of success are stated before testing.
- 4: One documented iteration driven by data.
- 3: DBTL is described, but the iterations are troubleshooting (re-running PCR) rather than redesign.
- 2: A DBTL diagram with nothing tested behind it.

a5 Human Practices (p.21-23: reflective, responsible, responsive; two-way dialogue)
- 5: HP shaped the design and execution. GreatBay: "Human Practices informed every aspect" (p.34). TAS: application thinking about real wastewater.
- 4: Several stakeholders, and at least one documented design change caused by them.
- 3: Interviews and surveys that are relevant but only loosely tied to decisions.
- 2: Outreach or marketing only, with no exchange between the project and the bigger picture (p.24).

a6 Own work (p.25-26 Attributions, now on the team page; p.31 "primarily by the students"; TAS: "the students themselves likely did most of the work" from figure captions and the attributions page)
- 5: Students designed and ran the experiments, and the attribution is specific to tasks.
- 4: Students did the core work. Defined pieces (sequencing, synthesis, one instrument run) are outsourced and declared.
- 3: Shared work, or key experiments run by mentors or a host lab.
- 2: Most of the execution was done by others, or the attribution is incomplete and the main tasks have no owner.

a7 SynBio and standard components (p.18-19; RFC10 / Type IIS RFC1000 screened automatically)
- 5: Engineered genetic devices built from Registry-compatible parts, with a new part plus reuse of existing ones. TAS: only the PR gene was new, but the project is "definitely based on synthetic biology and standard parts" (p.104).
- 4: A standard-part design with minor gaps.
- 3: Some synthetic biology content, but the standard parts are peripheral.
- 2: Mainly hardware or software, with nominal biology.

a8 Documentation (p.18: parts are judged on the Registry only, looking at sequence features, topology, host, rationale, experiments with controls, and characterisation; p.29: standard pages only)
- 5: Registry entries carry data and controls, and the wiki explains everything clearly from the standard pages.
- 4: Good wiki, but the Registry is thin for some parts.
- 3: The Registry has sequences and descriptions only, and the experimental data are on the wiki alone.
- 2: Parts are listed with no documentation, or key content is off-namespace or hidden.

w1 Communicates goals (Lambert_GA p.97: concise homepage, one schematic per idea; Patras p.95)
- 5: Problem, approach and outcome are clear within one screen.
- 4: Clear, with a little drift.
- 3: Understandable after some digging.
- 2: Jargon or hype hides what was done.

w2 Documented and supported by evidence (Lambert p.98: "rigorous experiments", setup, protocols, data analysis)
- 5: Every key claim has a figure with controls, replicates, a legend and methods.
- 4: Most do.
- 3: Some data, but missing legends, n, or controls.
- 2: Claims without data, or model output shown as a result.

w3 Design aids finding and understanding (Patras: side menu mapped to criteria, p.95-96)
- 5: Navigation follows the ballot, and the standard URLs are intact.
- 4: Easy to navigate, with minor friction.
- 3: Usable, but the key information is buried.
- 2: Sprawling, with broken or relocated standard pages.

w4 Record for future teams (digital p.94 "reconstruct the project from the ground up"; Lambert p.98)
- 5: Protocols, notebook, parts, raw data and failures are all present, so the project could be reproduced.
- 4: Mostly reproducible.
- 3: Results without the protocols needed to repeat them.
- 2: A showcase only.

w5 Referencing (digital p.94-95 Academic Integrity)
- 5: Every claim and image is cited to a resolvable source, and prior iGEM teams are credited (GreatBay p.34).
- 4: Small gaps.
- 3: A reference list only, with weak inline linking.
- 2: Uncited figures or claims, or citations that do not resolve.
memo.red_flags:
- A claim of "worked" or "successful" with no figure, table, gel or numbers. It does not count for a2 or w2.
- Modelled, simulated or planned results presented as experimental. I mark each one as modelled and score only the measured evidence. Digital p.95 classes AI-generated simulated results presented as data as misconduct.
- Missing controls, n = 1, no error bars, unlabelled gels, ladders with no size marks, or a photo of a well plate in place of plate-reader values (p.20-21).
- Part documentation that exists only on the wiki. p.18: judge the Registry only.
- Content on external sites (Google Drive, GitHub Pages, YouTube) or off the team namespace. Under p.29 it cannot be judged. Changed standard URLs, and material judges would have to hunt for.
- Execution outsourced to a university lab, a company or a mentor, or a vague attributions page (p.25-26, p.31). This lowers a6 and is not an integrity case in itself.
- For a High School team, organisms or activities outside the Whitelist: animals, most sporulating fungi, BSL-2 or higher, human samples (p.25). I raise these with safety@igem.org and do not decide them myself.
- Academic integrity issues (digital p.94-95): fabricated or non-resolving citations, AI-made or "cleaned" gels and plots, invented stakeholder quotes, plagiarism, AI-written substance. I report specific concerns to rcc@igem.org (digital p.94-95; p.25). I give no credit to evidence I cannot trust and make no accusation or penalty myself. The RCC decides.
- HP that is marketing or a "save the world" pitch with no two-way dialogue (p.23).
- Length used in place of quality. A sprawling wiki fails the digital p.94 test of "complete but not sprawling".
memo.not_observable:
- Presentation (four aspects, digital p.85-86): this simulation cannot see the videos. That comes from the simulation brief, not the handbook. Digital p.85 says that at a real Jamboree the videos "will be viewable to judges before the Grand Jamboree". I record Presentation as "not assessed" and do not infer a score from wiki polish. The weighted average therefore uses Project and Wiki only, under panel convention C1.
- Aspect 9 (Q&A): p.32 says judges "will primarily use the discussion time during the Judging Session". p.11 Step 3 says not to pre-fill items that depend on the Jamboree. I leave it blank and do not use a proxy for it.
- I do not score anything I cannot see: lab notebooks held off-wiki, external videos, or claims of private data. Where something matters, I write it down as a question I would ask the team.
- I note in every ballot that my ranking would be revised once the Presentation and Q&A were seen.
memo.memo:
J1 CALIBRATION MEMO: High School section, iGEM 2026 (wet-lab molecular biologist)

1. What decides the finalists
The handbook sets the rule. Finalists are the highest-ranking teams on the Project, Wiki and Presentation sections of the ballot (p.12, Step 8). The ranking uses a weighted average of those three, computed within each section. The High School section gets 2 finalists (p.28). Project "is the main determinant for choosing finalists" (p.31), but the handbook publishes no weights. Each team has six judges (p.27). Each vote is my own opinion and not a consensus (p.10, item 7). Awards need a minimum number of votes and a minimum score (p.28).

The simulation brief says we cannot see the Presentation videos. Digital p.85 says that in the real competition judges can view them before the Jamboree. So the missing Presentation score is a limit of this exercise, not handbook policy. I record Presentation as not assessed.

The panel conventions below are local to this simulation and are not handbook rules. All three judges need to agree on them.
- C1: composite = 0.7 × Project mean + 0.3 × Wiki mean.
- C2: Wiki is used second, as a tie-breaker.
- C3: if composites are within 0.25, compare a2, then a6, then a1.
- C4: a functioning-part benchmark, used for calibration only. Without one demonstrated working Part, a team rarely gets above 3 on a2. It never removes a team from consideration. The handbook calls a functioning Part "a substantial achievement" for a HS team (p.101). That describes an achievement, not a requirement.

2. High School calibration
Chapter 5 tells me to score HS teams "just as you would a standard collegiate team" and to "mark the ballot according to the language scale" (p.101). It also asks me to keep in mind smaller budgets, limited lab access and shorter hours. My 5s are pegged to the two HS Grand Prize case studies:
- GreatBay_SZ 2019 (p.32-35): spider silk expressed, spun, re-engineered and dyed. Failures discussed, iterative redesign, HP informing "every aspect", and a task-level attribution chart.
- TAS Taipei 2017 (p.102-104): PR citrate binding and curli-boosted biofilm, each tested against controls. Then a model used to fit parameters and build a dosing calculator, and a wastewater-style test that led to a design change (a biofilm carrier).

TAS shows that the parts do not have to be novel. Only one was new to the Registry. What carries a 5 is controls, a proof of concept, prototyping, and clear signs that students did the work. A 4 is clearly above the field with real data but one notch short of that coherence. A 3 is a competent medal-level project with partial function data. A 2 means the claims outrun the evidence.

3. What I look for first (my bias, made explicit so I can correct for it)
I go to Results, Engineering, Measurement and the Registry first. I check that:
- every "works" claim has a figure with a negative and a positive control;
- replicates are stated, n is given, error bars are defined and units are given;
- gels have size-marked ladders and named lanes;
- plate-reader data are normalised (OD, blank subtraction) and not shown as a well photo;
- modelled curves are clearly labelled as modelled.
p.20 rewards an honest qualitative result over a flawed quantitative one, and I will apply that. Because I lean toward the bench, I will also read HP (a5), impact (a3) and wiki design (w1, w3) closely enough to score them on their own merits. The handbook asks judges to be "master generalists" (p.8), and every aspect counts.

4. The exact aspect wording I score against
Project (p.31) includes a2 "Did the project work or is it likely to work?", a6 "How much of the work did the team do themselves and how much was done by others?" and a8 "Are the project components well documented on the team's Wiki/Registry pages (parts should be documented in the Registry)?" Wiki (digital p.94) includes w2 "Did the team clearly document their project and support their results with convincing experimental evidence?" and w3 "Does the design of the Wiki support visitors in finding and understanding the content?" Full wording and anchors are in the anchors field.

5. Evidence boundaries
- Only the wiki namespace, the Registry and iGEM GitLab count. I do not hunt for content, and standard URLs must be preserved (p.29).
- Parts are judged on the Registry entry alone: annotation, topology, host, rationale, experiments with controls, and characterisation (p.18). RFC10 and Type IIS compatibility is screened automatically (p.19).
- Attribution now appears on the team page (p.26). Outsourced execution lowers a6.
- HS teams must stay on the Whitelist: no animals, most sporulating fungi, BSL-2 or higher, or human samples (p.25). Questions go to safety@igem.org.

6. Integrity
Digital p.94-95 lists fabricated citations, AI-made or "cleaned" evidentiary figures, invented quotes, plagiarism, and AI-authored substance or simulated results presented as data. These "should be reported to the RCC". If I find a specific concern I email rcc@igem.org (also p.25). I give no evidential credit to material I cannot trust, and I score only what is documented. I do not exclude the team, accuse them or suggest a penalty myself. p.25 says it "is not up to judges" to do that, and the RCC decides. Finalist selection stays the weighted average (p.28).

7. What I cannot observe
- Presentation (four aspects, digital p.85-86) is not assessed, for the reason given in section 1.
- Aspect 9 is judged "primarily" in the Judging Session discussion (p.32). Following p.11 Step 3, I leave it blank.
- In each team's notes I list the questions I would ask in Q&A, and I flag that my ranking could change once the video and Q&A were seen.

8. Fairness and feedback
Length is not quality. A wiki should be "complete but not sprawling" (digital p.94). I apply the same evidence bar to every team and ignore reputation. Written feedback is specific and kind (p.13-15), and in my own words without AI-generated substance (p.10, item 10; p.15, Tip 6). High school students may still be deciding on a science career (p.101).

panel.lens: a bioprocess and hardware engineer from industry. You look first at the design-build-test-learn cycles, use of standards and modularity, whether the system is likely to work outside the lab, and how the pieces integrate into one working project.

memo.finalist_rule:
How the 2 High School finalists are chosen, from the handbook:
- p.12 (Quick Start, Step 8): "the highest ranking teams as determined by the 'Project', 'Wiki', and 'Presentation' sections of the ballot will become Finalists." They are announced Sunday 15 Nov, and the Grand Prize is voted at the final judge meeting on Monday 16 Nov, after a main-stage talk and a judging-room Q&A.
- p.28 ("Finalists"): finalists are the teams with the "highest score from a weighted average of these Rubric categories: Project, Presentation and Wiki, within each section". The high school section is ranked on its own and gets 2 finalists. The undergraduate section gets 3 and the overgraduate section gets 2.
- p.31: the Project section "is the main determinant for choosing finalists". The handbook does not publish the weights. I will treat Project as the heaviest weight, with Wiki and Presentation next.
- p.27: each team is scored by six judges with no known conflicts of interest, and each category uses that panel's votes. Judges must match their votes to the rubric language so scores are consistent across the judging body.
- p.28 (end): every award needs a minimum number of votes and a minimum score. A judge who abstains or votes carelessly can make a team ineligible, so I score every observable aspect.
- p.32: winners are the teams that impress the judges through the scale and scope of what they achieved, not through ticked boxes.
- Digital handbook Ch.5 p.101: judge HS teams "just as you would a standard collegiate team" and mark the ballot by the language scale. I still allow for HS limits: smaller budgets and labs, shorter hours, Whitelist organisms only (p.25). A working Part counts as "a substantial achievement".
- Ranking procedure for this panel: Presentation videos cannot be seen, so my Presentation score is "not assessed" and is never invented. The working rank is Project first, using the mean of a1-a8 with a1, a2 and a4 most decisive, then the Wiki mean (w1-w5) as the second key. When Project scores are close, the Wiki score breaks the tie. The top 2 by this rank are my proposed finalists.
memo.anchors:
Scale: 5 = finalist level for a high school team; 4 = strong, clearly above the field, with real evidence; 3 = solid medal-team work; 2 = present but thin, claims go beyond the evidence. Anchors: GreatBay_SZ 2019 (judge.txt p.32-35) and TAS Taipei 2017 (digital Ch.5 p.102-104).

a1 How impressive. 5: scale and scope at GreatBay level. GreatBay went through a chain of harder and harder steps (silk expression, then spinning on a modified rig, then repeat-number variants, then dyes, then fusions, then mixing) and told it as one story (p.33-34). TAS Taipei achieved "an impressive number of accomplishments" with high engineering quality (p.104). 4: two or three linked results with data, and one stage taken beyond the bench. 3: one clear goal, one or two results, and the rest planned. 2: an ambitious story where most of the work is design, modelling or intent.

a2 Did it work. 5: the main function is shown with controls and replicates. TAS Taipei shows an absorbance drop against a control strain plus a visible pellet (p.102), a biofilm proof of concept with an antibiotic-killed control, and a csgD/ompR234 combination that beats either gene alone (p.103). GreatBay also reports its failures, such as the insoluble red fusion (p.33). 4: at least one part works with quantitative data and controls, and the gaps are honestly marked. 3: construction is verified (gel or sequencing) and the function data are qualitative or preliminary. 2: "worked" is claimed with no figure, or the results are modelled. A working Part alone already counts strongly for a HS team (p.101).

a3 Impact. 5: credible use outside the lab, tested in a realistic setting. TAS Taipei ran a wastewater-style setup, found it insufficient, added a biofilm carrier, and showed fit with existing microbial treatment (p.104). 4: stakeholder-checked deployment route with concrete constraints. 3: the impact is plausible and argued from literature. 2: generic "save the world" claims, which p.23 warns against.

a4 Engineering. 5: real DBTL iterations that change the design. GreatBay "used iterative engineering to step back and fix parts" (p.34). TAS Taipei used controls, proof of concept, prototyping, and a model fitted to data then turned into a dose calculator (p.104). It also follows the p.17 method: quantified measures of success, assumptions stated, validation. 4: at least one complete cycle, where test data drive a redesign. 3: the DBTL is described, but cycles are mostly routine troubleshooting (p.14 warns about this). 2: a DBTL diagram with no test data behind it.

a5 Human Practices. 5: HP shapes every aspect. GreatBay consulted textile factories, technical experts and businesses (p.34). The p.21-22 criteria are reflective, responsible and responsive, with clear rationale for who was consulted and documented changes to the design. 4: several stakeholders, and at least one design change traced to them. 3: interviews and surveys that are reflective but loosely tied to design. 2: outreach or education presented as HP (p.24 says that does not count) or a list of contacts with no follow-up.

a6 Own work. 5: an attribution chart showing who did what (GreatBay p.34), figure captions and the attributions page showing students did most of the work (TAS Taipei p.104), and every field of the form complete (p.25). 4: clear attribution with modest outside help in the lab or on instruments. 3: idea and design are by students, but key steps (cloning, synthesis, measurement) were outsourced and say so. 2: vague attribution, or core execution by a lab or company.

a7 SynBio and standard parts. 5: built on standard parts with new parts in the Registry. TAS Taipei's parts were "not necessarily complicated" but standard and well documented, with one new part (p.104). A parts collection designed to be reused, or software, also counts (p.18). 4: new basic or composite parts that are RFC10/RFC1000 compatible and characterised. 3: existing parts reused, or one new part with light characterisation. 2: synthetic biology is peripheral, for example mostly hardware or chemistry, or no Registry parts.

a8 Documentation. 5: Registry pages have annotation, topology, host, rationale, experiments with controls, and characterisation (p.18), plus a wiki that lets someone rebuild the project. 4: most parts are documented on the Registry with data. 3: data are on the wiki but Registry entries are thin. Registry-only rule: I judge parts on the Registry, not the wiki (p.18). 2: Registry stubs only.

w1 Communication. 5: Lambert_GA style (digital p.97), with a concise concept on the home page, one sentence and one schematic per idea, and a clear description page. 3: the goal is clear but buried. 2: the reader cannot state the aim after reading the home and description pages.
w2 Evidence. 5: methods, protocols, graphs and analysis that validate the results (Lambert_GA p.98). 4: real data for the main claims. 3: some data, with gaps. 2: assertions, or modelled results only.
w3 Design and navigation. 5: Patras_Medicine (p.95-96), where a side menu maps to the judging criteria, the flow runs page to page, and the palette is accessible. 3: usable but sprawling. 2: key content hard to find, or the standard pages are empty.
w4 Record for future teams. 5: complete but not sprawling (p.94), with notebook, protocols, parts and modelling all on iGEM servers (Patras p.96). 3: partial. 2: a team could not reproduce the work from it.
w5 Citations. 5: every figure, prior iGEM work and claim is cited, and the references resolve (p.94). 3: a reference list with uneven in-text use. 2: few citations, or images without credit. Any fabricated citation is an integrity problem and goes outside this scale.
memo.red_flags:
- Unsupported claims: "it worked" or "successfully" with no figure, table, gel or numbers. This caps a2 and w2 at 2. Results with no controls or replicates are weaker (p.20-21 measurement questions; TAS Taipei was praised for its controls, p.104).
- Modelled, simulated or "expected" results presented as experimental. I label every result modelled, planned or measured. A model counts in a4 only if it predicts or explains measured data (p.17). A dose calculator built on fitted kinetics, as TAS Taipei did, is good. A calculator built on assumed constants is not evidence that the project works.
- Outsourced work: a CRO, university lab or company doing the cloning, synthesis or measurement. Instructors doing core execution. An attribution form with empty fields or "specific tasks" that do not match what was achieved (p.25-26). These lower a6, and a1 if the impressiveness rests on that work. I do not accuse anyone. I note it as a question and may refer it to the RCC (p.25).
- Content off the iGEM wiki: external sites, Google Drive, YouTube or GitHub cannot be judged (p.29). Parts documented only on the wiki and not on the Registry do not count for a7 or a8 (p.18). Supplementary pages count only if the standard pages link to them, because judges are not required to hunt (p.29).
- Academic integrity (digital p.94-95): fabricated or garbled citations, AI-generated or AI-cleaned evidence figures, invented "representative" stakeholder quotes, plagiarism, and AI-authored substance or simulated results. These are violations to report to the RCC, not just low scores. When I see a specific concrete indicator, I flag it to the panel and mark the aspects that rely on that content as unverified.
- Safety: a HS team using non-Whitelist organisms, BSL-2 work, animals or human samples (p.25). This goes to safety@igem.org.
- HP mislabelled: outreach or education with no exchange between the project and the bigger picture is not HP (p.24). Proselytising "SynBio saves the world" (p.23).
- Engineering theatre: DBTL diagrams with no test data, or "cycles" that are only repeated troubleshooting (p.14). Hardware claimed to work with no bench measurement, units or calibration (p.20: "measurements are the only way to show whether hardware is functioning").
- Length used in place of quality: a sprawling wiki with thin evidence scores below a concise one with strong data (digital p.94).
memo.not_observable:
- Project aspect 9 (Q&A competence): not scored. p.32 says it is judged mainly in the judging session. p.11 Step 3 says not to pre-fill questions that depend on Jamboree interaction. It stays blank. It does not become an implicit 0 or an assumed 3.
- Presentation section (4 aspects, digital p.85-86: communication with evidence, visual design, engagement, acknowledgement): videos are not visible to this panel, so it is recorded as "not assessed". I do not infer it from wiki polish. The finalist rank is computed from Project (a1-a8) and Wiki (w1-w5) only, and I say clearly that the official weighted average (p.28) also includes Presentation, which could reorder close teams.
- If a team's evidence appears to exist only in the video or the session (for example "we will show data at the Jamboree"), it does not count now. I note it as a follow-up question, as p.11 Step 2 says.
- Hardware demonstrations at booths are not judged (p.26). Only data documented on the wiki or Registry counts.
- Uncertainty: when an aspect depends on content I could not open (a broken page, or a JS-only page that did not render in the crawl), I try the live page in headless Chrome. If it still fails, I score only what I could read and note the gap. I do not penalise a rendering problem as if the content were absent without checking.
memo.memo:
J2 calibration memo: iGEM 2026 High School section (bioprocess and hardware engineer)

1. What I am deciding
I am proposing the 2 High School finalists. The handbook rule is short. Finalists are the "highest ranking teams as determined by the Project, Wiki and Presentation sections" (p.12, Step 8), using a weighted average of those three, ranked within the high school section, with 2 finalists (p.28). The Project section "is the main determinant for choosing finalists" (p.31). The weights are not published. Presentation videos are not visible to us, so my Presentation score is "not assessed" and I never invent one. My working rank is the Project mean (a1-a8) first, then the Wiki mean (w1-w5) as the second key and tie-breaker. Aspect 9, Q&A, stays blank (p.32; p.11 Step 3). I should tell the panel the official rank would also include Presentation, so close calls could flip.

2. What winning looks like for a high school team
Two anchors set the top of my scale.
GreatBay_SZ 2019 (p.32-35): spider silk in E. coli. They spun fibre on a rig adapted from a previous iGEM team, varied repeat number to tune the properties, built dye pathways, redesigned an insoluble blue dye with another team, and tried silk-dye fusions (GFP worked, red did not). They then switched to mixing separately purified proteins and made coloured fibres. The judges valued "a logical sequence of increasingly difficult steps", failures discussed openly, iterative engineering, HP that "informed every aspect" (textile factories, technical experts, businesses), and a who-did-what attribution chart.
TAS Taipei 2017 (digital Ch.5, p.102-104): nanoparticle capture. A proteorhodopsin strain was tested against a control. A biofilm proof of concept included an antibiotic-killed control. csgD and ompR234 each increased biofilm, and together they increased it more. Kinetic parameters were fitted and turned into a dose calculator. A wastewater-style setup was tested, found insufficient, and fixed with a biofilm carrier. The judges cited controls, proof of concept, prototyping and student-led work. They noted the parts were "not necessarily complicated" but standard and well documented.
What separates winners is being impressive (p.32): scale and scope of what was achieved in the time, not ticked boxes. The best engineered projects "don't try to take on too much" but define success criteria and deliver robust, characterised solutions (p.17). For a HS team, "it can be considered a substantial achievement... to make a functioning Part" (p.101). I credit one well-characterised working part strongly. Even so, the top HS teams compete with each other, and the finalists will be the ones that go further, toward a real-world test, a model fed by data, and redesign driven by data.

3. My lens, kept within the rubric
My background makes me look first at a4 (DBTL), a7 (standards and modularity), a2/a3 (will it work outside the lab) and how the pieces join up. I must not let that become a hardware bonus. Every aspect counts as the handbook says, including a5 (HP) and a6 (attribution), where I am less expert. I read HP against the p.21-23 reflective, responsible and responsive criteria, not against how much engineering it contains.
Engineering tests I will apply (p.15-17, p.20):
- Is there a stated, quantified measure of success, and was it measured?
- Did a test result cause a redesign? A real cycle changes the next build. Repeating a PCR until it works is troubleshooting (p.14).
- Is a model used to predict or explain data, or is it decoration? Was it fitted to their own measurements?
- Are there controls, replicates and units? Is it reproducible? Was it tested in more than one condition or host?
- For hardware or a bioreactor: calibration against a reference, sensor ranges and saturation, and a demonstration on real samples. "Measurements are the only way to show whether hardware is functioning correctly" (p.20).
- Modularity: RFC10/RFC1000-compatible parts, a collection designed for reuse, and a system whose subsystems were each validated and then integrated.

4. Evidence discipline
- No figure, table, gel or numbers means "claimed", not "worked".
- Every result gets one of three labels: measured, modelled or planned. Modelled and planned results never support a2.
- Parts are judged on the Registry only, not the wiki (p.18). Content off iGEM servers cannot be judged (p.29). I am not required to hunt beyond what the standard pages link to (p.29).
- Attribution is read from the team page form (p.26). I check whether every field is complete and the tasks plausible, and whether the core execution was by students. If outsourcing is declared, a6 goes down but there is no integrity issue. If outsourcing is undeclared but evident, I raise it as a question and may refer it to the RCC. I never make accusations (p.25).
- Academic integrity (digital p.94-95): fabricated citations, AI-made or AI-cleaned evidence figures, invented quotes and plagiarism are RCC matters. I flag specific indicators to the panel and mark the dependent aspects as unverified. A suspicion alone does not lower a score.
- Whitelist breaches go to safety@igem.org (p.25).
- Length is not quality. A great wiki is "complete but not sprawling" (p.94).

5. Scoring scale I will hold myself to
5 = a finalist at TAS Taipei or GreatBay level on that aspect. 4 = strong and clearly above the field, with real data. 3 = competent medal-team work. 2 = present but thin, claims ahead of evidence. 1 = token. 0 = absent. I use half points. I expect most teams to score 2.5-3.5. A 5 needs evidence I can point to by page and figure. Each 4 or 5 in my notes will name a specific figure or Registry part, and each 2 or below will name what is missing.
Wiki anchors: Patras_Medicine 2022 for navigation and keeping everything on iGEM servers (p.95-96). Lambert_GA 2022 for communication, documentation and evidence (p.97-98).

6. Procedure per team
1) Home and description pages: can I state the aim, the chassis, the parts and the success criterion? (w1)
2) Results, proof-of-concept, engineering and hardware pages: list each claim and label it measured, modelled or planned, with figure numbers. (a2, a4, w2)
3) Registry: the parts listed, their documentation depth, and compatibility. (a7, a8)
4) HP and implementation: who was consulted and why, and what changed in the design. (a5, a3)
5) Attributions form: completeness, and who did the execution. (a6)
6) Citations: spot-check that a few resolve and say what the wiki claims. (w5)
7) Score a1 last, as an overall judgement of scale and scope.
8) Record questions I would have asked in Q&A, without scoring them.

7. Fairness
I have no favourite team. Past reputation and wiki gloss do not earn points. I apply the same evidence standard to every team. Feedback is written by me, in my own words, kind but specific (p.13-15, p.10 rule 10). I remember these are high school students whose career choices my words may affect (digital p.101).

errors: Minor, invented sub-weighting: 'Project first, using the mean of a1-a8 with a1, a2 and a4 most decisive' has no basis in the handbook. p.31 makes the Project section the main determinant, but nothing in the handbook ranks aspects inside it. p.32 says excellent teams 'do not necessarily need to score highly in every aspect', and that the deciding factor is how impressive the work is. Using Wiki as the tie-breaker is also the panel's own procedure, not a handbook rule. The memo admits the weights are unpublished, so this is not fatal, but it should be labelled as panel convention.

Moderate narrowing of aspect 2: the handbook wording (p.31) is 'Did the project work or is it likely to work?'. The memo says 'Modelled and planned results never support a2', and its a2 scale ignores the 'likely to work' half. The brief's evidence rule (modelled is not experimental, and no data means not 'worked') is fine. But a team with partial measured data plus a well-grounded design or model can still earn credit for 'likely to work'. The memo should say this aspect is scored on 'worked or likely to work', with modelled support weighted below measured data, not shut out.

Misquote at p.20: the handbook reads 'Well-reported measurements are the only way to show whether hardware is functioning correctly'. The memo drops 'Well-reported' but keeps the quotation marks, in both red_flags and section 3.

Small citation and overreach slips: (a) 'software also counts (p.18)'. Software appears in the aspect 7 wording on p.31, not on p.18, which covers parts and part collections. (b) Saying parts documented only on the wiki 'do not count for a7' stretches p.18, which governs how Registry contributions and documentation (a8) are assessed. Aspect 7 asks whether the project is based on synthetic biology and standard components. (c) 'Supplementary pages count only if the standard pages link to them' is stronger than p.29, which says teams must guide judges and judges are not required to seek content out. It does not say unlinked team-namespace content is void. (d) The memo never states that iGEM GitLab content is judgeable. p.29 names Wiki, Registry and iGEM's GitLab as the permitted locations. GitHub is correctly listed as external.

panel.lens: a human practices, bioethics and science-education specialist who has judged iGEM high school teams before. You look first at whether stakeholder input really changed the design, at honest attribution of who did the work, and at how clearly the wiki communicates and cites.

memo.finalist_rule:
Judge-handbook rules, cited by page (judge.txt page markers; Chapters 4 and 5 by the printed page numbers in the digital copy):

1. Finalists come from the ballot, not from medals or special awards. Step 8 (p.12) says the highest-ranking teams on the "Project", "Wiki" and "Presentation" sections of the ballot become Finalists.
2. The formula is on p.28, under "Finalists": the highest score from a weighted average of the Project, Presentation and Wiki rubric categories, worked out within each section. High school is its own section. The High School section has exactly 2 finalists (undergraduate has 3, overgraduate 2). High school teams are not ranked against collegiate teams for this.
3. Weighting. The handbook does not publish the weights. P.31 says the Project section "is the main determinant for choosing finalists", so Project carries the most weight, with Wiki and Presentation behind it.
4. Each team has six judges (p.27). The award uses the panel's scores. Each vote is one individual judge's opinion and judges need not agree (p.10, rule 7). Every judge must vote in every visible category, or a team can lose eligibility. Every award also has a minimum number of votes and a minimum score (p.28).
5. Inside Project, aspect 9 (Q&A) is scored only at the Judging Session (p.32). Teams are not expected to max every aspect. "Impressing the judges is what distinguishes winning teams from great teams", judged on the scale and scope achieved in the time, not on ticked boxes (p.32).
6. Score high school teams on the same ballot language as collegiate teams. Keep in mind smaller budgets, fewer labs and shorter hours: "it can be considered a substantial achievement for a high school team to make a functioning Part". The top HS teams can be hard to tell apart from collegiate teams (Ch.5, p.101).
7. Process for this exercise: score a1-a8 and w1-w5 for every team. Record Presentation and a9 as NOT ASSESSED. Rank first on the Project average (a1-a8), then use the Wiki average to separate close teams. Nominate the top 2. Where the two are close on Project, state openly that a missing Presentation score could reorder them.
memo.anchors:
The anchors come from GreatBay_SZ 2019 (p.32-35), TAS Taipei 2017 (Ch.5 p.102-104), GreatBay-SCIE 2025 for integrated HP (p.66-67), the Engineering, Parts, Measurement, HP and Attribution guidance (p.15-26), and Patras_Medicine 2022 and Lambert_GA 2022 for the wiki (p.95-98). Half points are allowed.

PROJECT
a1 Impressive
5: covers a lot and climbs logically through harder and harder steps to a coherent story with elegant results, all within one season. Examples: GreatBay silk, then spinning, then optimised repeat variants, then dyes, then colour mixing (p.33-34); TAS with two working mechanisms plus a model, a calculator and a wastewater prototype (p.103-104).
4: one mechanism carried convincingly from design to data, plus one extra layer (a model used for design, a prototype or hardware).
3: a sensible idea, carried through to partial data.
2: an ambitious story whose evidence stops at cloning or at plans.

a2 Worked / likely to work
5: the core parts clearly work, with controls and time courses, and a picture or measurement a reader can check. TAS showed absorbance dropping against a control strain and darker pellets, and its biofilm genes beat the control both alone and combined (p.102-103). Failures are reported honestly (p.34).
4: the main device works, shown by replicated quantitative data with controls, though secondary goals are unproven.
3: a construct was built and confirmed (gel or sequencing) and there is preliminary function data with weak controls or n=1.
2: only cloning, or the claims of function rest on modelled or expected results.

a3 Impact
5: a credible route into a real system, tested in something close to the real setting, and stakeholders confirm the need. TAS: microbes already sit in wastewater treatment, and the team adapted its system to sedimentation tanks with a biofilm carrier (p.104). GreatBay: textile factories (p.34).
4: a real need confirmed by users, plus a concrete deployment plan that names its limits.
3: a plausible need backed only by literature.
2: generic "save the world" framing (warned against on p.23).

a4 Engineering
5: several genuine DBTL loops in which a failure led to a redesign. GreatBay redesigned the insoluble blue dye construct with another team, and when the red fusion failed it switched to separate expression (p.33-34). TAS used controls, a proof of concept before building, and prototyping (p.104). The model is fitted to the team's own data and then used for design (TAS kinetic parameters and calculator). The team also defines measures of success and its assumptions (p.17).
4: one complete, documented cycle in which a Learn step actually changed the next Build, with quantitative success criteria.
3: DBTL is described, but it reads as routine troubleshooting (p.14).
2: a DBTL diagram with no data behind the iteration.

a5 Human practices
5: HP shapes every aspect of the project (GreatBay p.34). Stakeholder feedback turns into concrete changes in a documented reflection loop (GreatBay-SCIE: a survey led to non-toxic components and a fragrance, p.67). Critical voices are consulted, negative impacts and misuse are anticipated, and surveys follow the ethics rules and validity practice for minors (p.21-24).
4: two or more named design changes, each traceable to a specific stakeholder, with a rationale for why those stakeholders were chosen.
3: a broad set of interviews with thoughtful reflection, but the project would look the same without them.
2: a list of contacts or outreach events with no exchange between project and world. That is outreach, not HP (p.24).

a6 Own work
5: a chart of which student did what. External help, past iGEM teams and references are acknowledged, and figure captions and the Attributions form agree that students did most of the bench and analysis work (GreatBay p.34; TAS p.104; form requirements p.25-26, p.42).
4: clear attribution of the main tasks to students, with outside help bounded and named.
3: the form is filled in but vague, and some key steps are done by a host lab or company.
2: synthesis, assays or modelling done largely by others, or attribution missing or unclear for the essential work.

a7 Synthetic biology and standard parts
5: the design is built from standard parts in RFC10/RFC1000-compatible form. It contributes at least one new or improved functional part and uses existing parts well. TAS had only one new part but "definitely based on synthetic biology and standard parts" (p.104). Software or hardware can count as standard components (p.31).
4: designed composite parts, at least one of them shown to work.
3: standard parts assembled, but little new design.
2: synthetic biology is peripheral, or the parts were designed but never built.

a8 Wiki and Registry documentation
5: parts documented on the Registry itself with sequence features, topology, host, rationale, experiments with controls, and characterisation. Collection-level documentation where relevant (p.18). The wiki gives figure captions, protocols and raw data. TAS parts were "well-documented in the Registry" (p.104).
4: the main parts are documented on the Registry with real data, though minor parts are thin.
3: entries exist but carry little data, and the data live only on the wiki. Wiki-only documentation does not count for parts (p.18).
2: stub entries, or parts named but not registered.

WIKI
w1 Communicates goals
5: the home page states problem, approach and goal in a few lines with a schematic, then guides the reader onward (Lambert_GA, Patras p.95-97).
4: clear, with minor digressions.
3: the goal is clear only after several pages.
2: jargon-heavy, or the goal is unclear.

w2 Documented with convincing experimental evidence
5: every claim is backed by a figure with controls, units and n. Results are clearly separated from model outputs and plans (Lambert_GA "rigorous experiments… well-documented results", p.98).
4: the main claims are backed by data, with gaps acknowledged.
3: some data, mixed with unsupported claims.
2: mostly narrative, or simulated results presented as results.

w3 Design and navigation
5: standard pages kept, the side menu maps onto the judging criteria, and the wiki is "complete but not sprawling" (p.94-95).
4: easy to navigate, with minor dead ends.
3: usable, but content is buried or off the standard pages.
2: judges have to hunt for material, against the rule on p.29.

w4 Record for future teams
5: everything needed to rebuild the project is there: protocols, notebook, raw data, parts, safety, who did what, all on iGEM servers (p.94, p.96).
4: mostly reproducible.
3: protocols are thin or missing.
2: a showcase only.

w5 References and citations
5: every image, prior iGEM team and paper is cited, each reference resolves, and the cited claim is really in the source (Academic Integrity p.94).
4: consistent citations with minor lapses.
3: a reference list exists, but in-text links are patchy or images are uncredited.
2: few citations, or prior iGEM work not acknowledged.
memo.red_flags:
1. Claims without data. "Worked", "successfully" or "validated" with no figure, gel, table, numbers or controls shown counts as not worked (brief evidence rules; p.20-21 Measurement). It caps a2 and w2 at 2.
2. Modelled, simulated, expected or "representative" results written up as experimental results. If a projected yield, "expected results" figure or dose calculation carries no label, mark down a2, w2 and a4. Producing simulated results with AI is research misconduct and goes to the RCC (Responsible AI, p.94-95).
3. Outsourced work. Look for synthesis, cloning, assays, modelling or hardware done by a host university lab, a company or instructors. Also look for an Attributions form with blank "Specific Tasks", vague wording like "the team", or claims that do not match what the students could plausibly have done (p.25-26, p.42). This lowers a6. If honesty is in doubt, seek clarification at the session or contact rcc@igem.org. Judges do not accuse (p.25).
4. Content off the iGEM wiki. Google Drive links, external sites, YouTube, GitHub and similar cannot be judged (p.29). Score only what is on 2026.igem.wiki/<team>, the Registry and iGEM GitLab. Part documentation that lives only on the wiki does not meet the parts requirements (p.18).
5. Academic integrity (p.94). Watch for citations that do not resolve or do not support the claim, gel, plot or microscopy images that look AI-generated or "cleaned", invented or "representative" stakeholder quotes, and text, figures or code copied from another team, the literature or an AI without attribution. Each of these must be reported to the RCC. They pull down w5, w2, a5 (quotes) and a6. When I suspect one, I write down the specific evidence instead of guessing.
6. AI-authored substance. When the reasoning and project choices are not in the team's own voice (p.94-95), I treat it as an attribution question and do not invent a penalty. If the wiki discloses AI use for polish, that is acceptable.
7. Human practices that is only outreach: events with no exchange between project and world (p.24), stakeholder lists with no design consequence, marketing iGEM or synthetic biology to communities (p.23), and surveys of minors with no mention of ethics oversight (p.23).
8. Safety. Work outside the Whitelist, such as animals, BSL-2 organisms or human samples (p.25), is a serious flag and gets referred to safety@igem.org.
9. Sprawl. Length is not quality. A long wiki with thin evidence ranks below a concise one with strong data ("complete but not sprawling", p.94).
memo.not_observable:
Presentation (all four aspects, p.85): the videos are not public to us, so I record NOT ASSESSED and give no score, not even a neutral default. Q&A, Project aspect 9 (p.32): it is scored only at the Judging Session, and Quick Start Step 3 says not to pre-fill session-dependent items (p.11). I record NOT ASSESSED.

How I deal with the gap:
(a) I rank on Project a1-a8 as the main determinant (p.31), with Wiki as the secondary input.
(b) I do not let a guess about the video leak into Wiki or Project scores. "Teams probably explain it better in the video" never lifts a2.
(c) I flag any finalist decision with a narrow margin (about 0.3 points or less on the Project average) as liable to change with Presentation and Q&A, and I name the runner-up.
(d) I keep a short list of questions per team for the session, for example "Who ran this assay?", "Is this figure measured or modelled?" and "Which stakeholder changed which design choice?". These are things I would settle in Q&A, not penalise now.
(e) Missing Attributions-form detail on the wiki is not itself penalised in 2026, because the form now lives on the team page (p.26, p.42). If I cannot see the form, I score a6 from the wiki's own attribution and captions and note that the form was not checked.
memo.memo:
CALIBRATION MEMO: J3 (HP, bioethics and science education), iGEM 2026 High School section

What I am deciding. Two high school finalists, chosen within the HS section by a weighted average of Project, Presentation and Wiki (p.12 Step 8; p.28). Project is "the main determinant" (p.31), so the Project aspects a1-a8 drive my ranking and Wiki w1-w5 refines it. Presentation and Q&A (a9) are NOT ASSESSED; I never invent a number for them. Where my top two are close, I say that the missing Presentation could reorder them.

The bar. My 5 is GreatBay_SZ 2019 or TAS Taipei 2017 on that aspect. GreatBay (p.32-35) climbed through harder and harder steps: silk, spinning, repeat-number variants, dyes, colour mixing. It reported failures (an insoluble blue dye, an unspinnable red fusion) and redesigned around them. HP "informed every aspect" (textile factories, technical experts, businesses), and a chart showed who did what. TAS (p.102-104) showed working parts with controls (absorbance falling against a control strain; csgD and ompR234 each raising biofilm, more so combined) and ran a proof of concept before building. It fitted kinetic parameters to its own data and turned them into a dosing calculator, then tested a wastewater-style setup and changed the design (a biofilm carrier) as a result. Its parts were not complicated, with only one new to the Registry, and it still won. That tells me to reward depth, evidence and honest iteration over novelty or ambition. "It can be considered a substantial achievement for a high school team to make a functioning Part" (p.101), so one well-characterised working part with controls is already 4-level work on a2. But the best HS teams are compared with each other, and with collegiate quality (p.101).

My lens and its limits. I look first at three things.
(1) Whether stakeholder input really changed the design. For a5 I want a traceable chain: who was consulted, why that stakeholder, what they said, what changed, and how the team reflected on the trade-off (p.21-23; GreatBay-SCIE 2025 4A loop, p.67). A long contact list with no consequence is a 2-3. Outreach with no exchange between project and world is not HP at all (p.24). It belongs on Education or Inclusivity and does not count toward a5.
(2) Honest attribution. a6 rewards clear accounts of student work, not modesty or bravado. Captions saying who ran each experiment, a who-did-what chart, and named external help are the GreatBay and TAS pattern (p.34, p.104). Vague "the team did everything" alongside sophisticated host-lab methods lowers a6 and becomes a session question, not an accusation (p.25).
(3) Communication and citation (w1, w5). I check that references resolve and say what is claimed (Academic Integrity, p.94).
My background does not change the weights. A team with brilliant HP and no working biology cannot outrank a team with working parts. I deliberately score a2, a4, a7 and a8 as hard as a5, and I use the Engineering (p.15-18), Parts (p.18-19) and Measurement (p.20-21) guidance for them.

Evidence discipline.
- A claim only counts with a figure, gel, table or numbers, and with controls where function is claimed. Qualitative but honest beats flawed quantitative (p.20).
- Modelled, expected or planned outcomes are labelled as such in my notes and never counted toward a2 or w2. A model scores in a4 only if it predicted, guided or explained the team's own system (p.17). TAS's calculator is the model to beat.
- I cite the wiki page for every key piece of evidence. If I cannot find it from the standard pages, it does not exist for scoring (p.29). External links, Drive files and videos hosted elsewhere are ignored. Part documentation must be on the Registry (p.18): wiki-only part data caps a8 at 3.
- Length is not quality. "Complete but not sprawling" (p.94) is the wiki ideal. I discount padding, generic background and repetition. A concise wiki with real data beats a long, glossy one.
- Integrity flags I watch for: unresolvable or misattributed citations; evidentiary figures that look generated or cleaned; "representative" stakeholder quotes; copied text or figures with no credit; AI-authored reasoning presented as the team's voice (p.94-95). If I see one, I record the specific evidence and lower the affected aspects (w5, w2, a5, a6). Genuine violations are reported to the RCC rather than quietly penalised. Disclosed AI use for polish is acceptable.
- Surveys and interviews with minors or the public should mention consent and ethics or oversight (p.23-24). Their absence is a reflective gap in a5, not an automatic zero.
- Whitelist breaches (animals, BSL-2, human samples, p.25) go to safety@igem.org.

Scoring procedure per team.
1. Read the Description, Engineering, Results/Proof of Concept, HP, Attributions/Team, Parts and Model pages, then follow links to Registry entries.
2. List each claim and classify it as MEASURED (with figure), MODELLED, or PLANNED.
3. Score a1-a8 against the anchors with half points. a1 is a holistic judgement of scale and scope, not a sum of the others (p.32).
4. Score w1-w5.
5. Write one strength and one constructive point per section. The writing must be mine, specific and kind, because these are high school students deciding on science careers (p.101, p.13-15).
6. Record Presentation and a9 as NOT ASSESSED, plus two or three questions for the session.

Separating the top two. Among the strongest HS wikis, I rank by Project average, asking in order:
- Does the core biology demonstrably work, with controls (a2)?
- Did the team iterate on failure (a4)?
- Did HP change the design (a5)?
- Did students do it (a6)?
- Can a future team reuse it from the Registry (a8)?
Wiki average breaks ties within about 0.3. Team fame, past results, polish and word count earn nothing. I judge only the 2026 wiki in front of me, with the same severity for every team.

Calibration self-checks. A 5 should be rare: if more than one or two teams get a 5 on any aspect, I am too lenient. If a team has no measured functional data, a2 is 2.5 or below whatever the narrative says. If HP changed nothing in the design, a5 is 3 or below. If I cannot tell who did the bench work, a6 is 3 or below until the session clarifies. I re-read my two finalists' Results pages last to confirm the evidence I cited is really there.

challenges.argument:
OVERRATED CASE (survives, narrowly): the rank-1 team did none of its own construction. experiments.txt:184 states flatly 'No cloning was carried out in this project. Every construct was synthesised and supplied as a sequence-verified plasmid', engineering.txt:155 repeats it, competent cells came from the Amgen programme and the supervisor prepared every mercury solution. The Team page assigns no student to wet lab at all - every role is Human Practice, Product Design, Conceptualization or Wiki Coding - and attributions.txt is an empty iframe shell, so the wiki itself contains no evidence of who ran the assays, the ImageJ analysis or the hardware builds. J2 reports the external form credits a secondary PI with hardware design, software and wiki writing; that cannot be checked from the wiki, which is the judgeable source (p.29). a6 scores of 4.0/3.5/3.5 are therefore generous: this is 'key steps outsourced', and the outsourced steps include all of construction plus, possibly, the engineering that makes the project look impressive. Entrepreneurship prose ('highly accurate', 'exact mercury number') also contradicts the lab pages, and the stated aim of an equipment-free visual readout is not met (colour needs a centrifuge above ~0.5 uM).

UNDERRATED CASE (fails to overturn): the project nonetheless has the single best-supported central claim in the field. Five matched independent runs, 51/51 treatments above matched controls in both pellet readouts, paired t-tests at the lowest tested concentration, selectivity against three metals in all eight matched comparisons, a calibration model fitted on four runs and tested on two withheld ones with RMSE in uM, and an independently built instrument reproducing the dose response at R2 = 0.9898. Nobody else in the top six replicated their headline result five times.

VERDICT: the overrated case survives only as a 0.3-0.5 correction to a6, not to a2. Replication is the rarest commodity here and this team has it; outsourcing construction costs one aspect out of eight.

challenges.argument:
OVERRATED CASE (survives): the project's defining mechanism is not demonstrated, and the wiki's own front matter says otherwise. results.txt:15 puts 'Light control - Green light switches ACCD on' in the Key results banner of the Results page; Figures 22 and 24 show ELISA flat at 2.6-3.2 and 12-13 ug/mL under green and red alike, Fig 25 shows DNPH inverting between 13 h and 16 h, and line 412 records red light BEATING green at 3 h in the pre-cultured set. The team's own closing paragraph (results.txt:258) concedes the data 'do not yet show a clean, graded response' and that the red LEDs are at 640 nm rather than the ~672 nm CcaSR needs. An abstract-level claim contradicted by the figures beneath it is exactly what w2 and a2 are meant to catch, and three judges gave w2 4.5 across the board. Add: attributions.txt is 141 words of navigation with no content, so with six instructors, four returning student advisors, a weekly NTU postdoc and three DNA vendors in play there is no attribution statement anywhere; several load-bearing numbers are n = 1 (secreted activity 7.25 mU/mL, both containment platings); the system is never joined end to end; and two of the team's own pages disagree on payback by 14x (68 years vs 4.9).

UNDERRATED CASE (real, and partly survives): the pre-registered growth-rate prediction (written 1 October, scored against run 6 thirteen days later, secondary endpoints declared unscorable in advance) is better practice than most collegiate teams manage, and the membrane result is complete on its own terms - anti-His blot across lysate/lumen/shell, active enzyme at 6-8 U/mg in the cell-free permeate for 72 h, no shell-side colonies. Plant rescue is replicated at n = 9-40 with mock and plasmid-free controls and includes an inconvenient negative. The hardware DBTL record is the strongest on the ballot.

VERDICT: both survive in part, but they do not cancel. The pre-registration is a growth-rate prediction, i.e. a prediction about a logistic fit, not about the project's function; the function itself is the thing that failed. A project whose headline mechanism is unshown should not out-rank one whose headline mechanism is replicated five times.

challenges.argument:
OVERRATED CASE: the headline application claim is a null. results.txt:335 records that after Holm correction 'none of these comparisons reached significance', with the best figure, W9 against untreated oak, at adjusted p = 0.194 on n = 3; the char difference is Welch p = 0.038 but permutation p = 0.10; and the marketed comparator also fails to separate from bare wood in the same rig, which indicts the apparatus. The enzyme was never assayed - results.txt:446 concedes the Western 'shows that the tagged protein is present, which is not the same as showing that it is folded and catalytically active' - and the coating used crude lysate of unmeasured melanin content with the decisive empty-vector-extract control never run (results.txt:450). Scope is also the narrowest of the top six: no model, no hardware, no software. Against a1 anchors that reward scale, 4.125 project is at the top of what this supports.

UNDERRATED CASE (stronger than it looks): the production half is the cleanest causal chain in the whole field - anti-His blot with both empty-vector and no-copper lanes, pigment index above empty vector at all four substrate levels with n = 3 independent cultures and Holm p = 0.0011-0.0118, and 4.19 +- 0.34 mg recovered against 0.03 +- 0.01 mg for empty vector with a spectral slope within 0.5% of an authentic Sepia standard carried through the entire procedure. The statistics are the only ones on the ballot that report raw and corrected p-values side by side, prefer CIs at n = 3, and run a permutation check against their own favourable result. Two failed Bradford curves and eleven of eighteen extrapolated values are published rather than buried. And unlike hongkong-jss and labi-taiwan, these students did their own bench work from a standing start.

VERDICT: the two cases cancel almost exactly, which is why the zero-spread 4.169 looks right. The null result is reported so well that it is evidence of judgement rather than failure; but a null is still a null, and it caps a3/a2. Leave as scored. Note for the panel: J2 and J3 report that all five Registry entries name the instructor as sole designer with Conceptualization and Investigation roles and no student credited - I could not verify this (Registry unreachable), but if true it contradicts J1's a6 = 4.5 and is worth a Q&A question.

challenges.argument:
OVERRATED CASE (survives): three separate dependencies sit under the rank-4 placing. (1) Construction was entirely external - parts.txt:140 states 'The complete plasmids were synthesized and cloned by Twist Bioscience', so like hongkong-jss this team did no cloning. (2) The ML tool that is the project's most distinctive asset was trained on someone else's data: parts.txt:50 says 'The TWJ model was trained using data from our previous wet-lab screening (last year team taipei-kcislk-v3)'. (3) J1 and J3 scored a6 from the external iGEM attribution form stating the PI designed the experimental workflow, wrote the protocols and ran most preliminary experiments before student implementation - but the wiki's own attributions page is empty (69 words, nav only), and p.29 limits judging to the wiki, Registry and GitLab. Two judges credited a disclosure a third could not read, and the disclosure itself is damaging. On top: the sensing chain is never closed (sfGFP never replaced by AciI, electrode never driven by the biology), the integration claim rests on one low-signal run at 1 nM that the team itself calls 'an initial proof of concept' (results.txt:308-309), nothing was tested in any matrix, and the Hardware page is aspirational - 'we aim to develop the BlueCatcher application' (hardware.txt:70) - with no measured data.

UNDERRATED CASE: the Human Practices work is genuinely the best on the ballot (J3 gave it a 5 and I would not argue), with four AREA phases each closing on a reversal traceable to a named person, and the dry lab is real - GEO reprocessing, an ML model tested prospectively on designs absent from training, and an SWV calibration rebuilt after a failed first series.

VERDICT: the overrated case survives. Strip the predecessor team's dataset, the vendor's cloning and the PI's protocol design, and what remains is excellent screening and excellent HP around a device that was never assembled. The 0.5 spread (J1 4.313 vs J2 3.813) is the table's largest and is explained precisely by whether a judge read the external form; it should be resolved toward J2.

challenges.argument:
OVERRATED CASE: the headline functional assay has no non-engineered arm. The Cycle 4 ICP-OES panel compares engineered strains against the starting standard only, with no wild-type K. rhaeticus, no empty-vector biomass and no cellulose-only control, and no replicate count or error bars anywhere - while results.txt:139 and engineering.txt:293 claim the mass balance 'rigorously proves that captured metal ions are specifically immobilized onto the bacterial cellulose matrix'. A mass balance is an accounting identity; it is logically incapable of establishing specificity, and the team's own Contribution page says so ('It does not show that the peptide is the only thing binding it', contribution.txt:188) and Part Collection repeats it (x__part_collection.txt:224). Bare bacterial cellulose sorbs metal ions, so the capture may be the chassis, not the payload. Single-step Li removal of 12.75-19.14% is modest, nothing was tested in anything resembling a tail stream, and there is no model of any kind.

UNDERRATED CASE (partly survives): the specificity objection is overstated by all three judges. The eight-strain panel is a within-scaffold, within-chassis head-to-head of paired peptide variants (e.g. MnBP1 35.50% vs MnBP2 41.10% single-step removal at 10 mg/L), and that comparison does control for native cellulose and cell-surface sorption - it is the peptide that differs. The defect is that these are single unreplicated values, so the difference is uninterpretable, not that the design is uncontrolled. Separately, this team has the best attribution record of the six (30 itemised entries, three AI tools scoped, the sponsor's laboratory declared) against two empty attribution pages and one unreadable iframe above it; a genuinely non-model chassis; a 27-part collection built for reuse and demonstrated by payload swap; and twelve industry interviews that moved the target user twice.

VERDICT: fair where it sits. The a2/w2 penalty for the missing control is right, but a6 at 4.0-4.5 is if anything under-credited relative to the teams above it, and that offsets. The pages that contradict each other on 'rigorously proves' should be a Q&A question about which page the team stands behind.

Uncleaned drafting or template instructions remain in the published Engineering page - 'Each map should identify the candidate coding sequence, promoter, relevant fusion or affinity tags, antibiotic-resistance marker, and plasmid size' (engineering.txt:127) and 'The final reporting unit must reflect the normalization actually used' (:225). The four modules were never run together, and hair degradation is an A280 proxy plus micrographs, never mass lost.

The 'Result Claim / Observation / Limitations' blocks are good practice.

VERDICT: overrated. J1's wiki 4.4 is indefensible against template remnants and a Safety page that contradicts the Results page; J2 and J3 at 3.9/4.1 are closer. The project mean of 3.979 is about right; the wiki mean should come down.

CHECKED AS THE STRONGEST 'UNDERRATED LOWER TEAM' CANDIDATE and rejected. plklfc has the highest project mean outside the top five (4.083, above basis-china's 3.979 at rank 6) and is held down almost entirely by a wiki mean of 3.767, so under the handbook's statement that Project 'is the main determinant for choosing finalists' (p.31) it has a prima facie case for promotion. skeptic.verdict_on_top2:
The #1 placing survives; the #2 placing does not, and the panel should not treat it as settled.

First place (hongkong-jss, 4.239) holds. Its margin over gems-taiwan is 0.070, which is smaller than its own inter-judge spread (0.072) and would normally be noise - but the two teams fail in asymmetric ways and the asymmetry favours hongkong-jss. Both have an attribution hole (hongkong-jss's page is an unreadable iframe with no student assigned to wet lab; gems-taiwan's is 141 words of navigation). Both outsourced heavily. The difference is at aspect 2. hongkong-jss's central claim is characterised in five matched independent runs with 51/51 treatments above matched controls, selectivity against three metals in all eight matched comparisons, a calibration model validated on two withheld runs, and an independently built instrument reproducing the dose response - the only properly replicated headline result among the finalists. gems-taiwan's central claim, light control of protectant production, is contradicted by its own figures while its Results banner asserts it plainly (results.txt:15 against Figs 22-25). A project that proves a smaller thing is worth more than a project that asserts a larger thing, and the handbook's evidence rule is explicit that a claim without supporting data does not count as having worked. I would apply roughly -0.05 to hongkong-jss (a6, for doing no cloning) and -0.08 to gems-taiwan (a2 and w2, for the unsupported headline), which widens rather than closes the gap.

Second place is unstable in three ways and should go to the Presentation and Q&A to break. (1) gems-taiwan and korea-hs are tied to three decimal places at 4.169, from completely different score profiles - gems on scale with an unproven mechanism, korea-hs on a narrow but rigorously evidenced production chain with a null application result. The tie is real, not a rounding artefact. (2) korea-hs's three judges returned identical ballots (spread 0.000), which is either unusual agreement or insufficient independence; gems-taiwan's spread is 0.122 and labi-taiwan's is 0.500, the table's largest. (3) My corrections move labi-taiwan down (-0.10, to about 4.04) and leave korea-hs where it is, so the second slot comes down to gems-taiwan versus korea-hs on judgement rather than arithmetic.

On that judgement I would put korea-hs second. gems-taiwan's advantages - twelve DBTL cycles, four instruments, a pre-registered prediction - are advantages in aspects 1 and 4, and its pre-registration scores a logistic growth fit rather than any project function. Its aspect 2, aspect 6 and w2 all rest on material that does not hold: a headline mechanism its own data contradict, containment on two unreplicated platings, several load-bearing n = 1 values, and no attribution statement at all. korea-hs proves less but proves it, reports its failures with raw and corrected p-values side by side, and is the only one of the three where the students demonstrably did their own bench work. If the panel disagrees and seats gems-taiwan second on scale, it should at minimum put the empty attribution page and the 'Green light switches ACCD on' banner to the team directly in Q&A.

No team below rank 6 belongs in the finalist conversation: plklfc, the best candidate on project mean, has no attributions page at all alongside mammalian cancer-cell work of unstated provenance, and greatbay-scie has no Results page.
